steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Sound in film is divided into diegetic, originating from within the film world, and non-diegetic, added for the audience from outside the narrative world.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Diegetic sound includes dialogue, ambient sound, on-screen music and sound effects that characters can theoretically hear.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Non-diegetic sound includes the musical score, voice-over narration and sound effects added for dramatic effect that characters cannot hear.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Sound can be further divided into on-screen and off-screen, with off-screen sound extending the diegetic world beyond the visible frame.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always specify whether sound is diegetic or non-diegetic — this is a fundamental distinction examiners look for. When discussing music, identify whether it is diegetic or non-diegetic and explain the significance of the distinction. Analyse the effect of silence — it is a deliberate sound choice, not an absence of technique. Link sound to other film elements: how does the score work with the editing pace? How does dialogue complement the mise-en-scene? Use the terms 'parallel' and 'contrapuntal' rather than vague descriptions like 'the music fits' or 'the music doesn't match'.
